prompt: A small clinic's front desk uses an AI tool three different ways in one week: (1) someone types a patient letter into a chat window and asks it to sound warmer, (2) the booking website quietly rewrites appointment confirmation texts before sending them, using AI wired directly into the booking software with no chat window anywhere, (3) a developer friend writes a short program that sends the day's no-show list to an AI provider's API and gets back a drafted reminder message for each one, ready to review. Which of these is the *embedded feature*?

options.text: The chat window where someone types the patient letter
The booking website rewriting confirmation texts with no chat window in sight
The developer's program that calls the API for reminder drafts
All three — embedded just means "AI is involved somewhere"

hints: Ask who is typing the prompt, and where.
An embedded feature is one where somebody else already wrote the prompt and wired it into a button or a workflow you didn't design.
explanation: The booking site is the embedded feature: the AI is stitched into an existing piece of software at a specific point, and the person receiving the confirmation text never sees a chat box, a prompt, or a choice about it — someone else built that decision in. The chat window is the plain chat pattern: a human typing into a conversational interface, turn by turn. The developer's program is an API call: code sending a request and getting text back, with no visible chat interface, driven by someone who wrote the request themselves rather than clicking a feature someone else shipped. The distractor — "all three" — is tempting because AI genuinely is involved in all three, but the four patterns aren't about whether AI is present, they're about *how a human or a system reaches it*, and that's a different question with a real answer in each case.

prompt: A freelance bookkeeper wants to "use AI" to help clients categorise their expenses. She could: type each month's transaction list into a chat window herself; pay for a bookkeeping app that has AI categorisation built in already; or have someone build her a small program that sends each transaction to an AI API and gets a category back automatically. Pick the one you'd actually recommend for someone with about 40 clients and no technical background of her own, and say what would make you change your answer.
hints: Forty clients a month is a lot of repetition — what does that do to the case for typing things into a chat window by hand?
"No technical background of her own" doesn't rule out a script or an embedded feature — it rules out her personally maintaining one.
What would change the answer: does she need something today, or is it worth a week's setup for years of use?
explanation: The bookkeeping app with built-in AI categorisation is usually the right call at this scale: 40 clients means the task repeats constantly, ruling out hand-typing into chat as unsustainable, but she also has no technical background and no team to build or maintain a custom script — so a purpose-built embedded feature, made by people whose job is to keep it working, fits better than either extreme. The case for a custom API-driven script strengthens sharply if her needs are unusual enough that no off-the-shelf tool covers them (an odd category scheme a specific client insists on, say), because then she's paying either way — in awkward manual work with the app, or in setup cost for something exact. There's no single right answer at every scale; the point is naming which factor — volume, maintenance capacity, and how standard the need is — is actually driving the choice, rather than picking whichever pattern sounds most "AI."

prompt: Sort each real situation into the pattern it actually is.

items.text: Typing a question into Claude.ai and reading the reply
A grammar-checking browser extension that underlines suggested edits directly in your email draft, no separate window
A support ticket system where, when a ticket comes in, code sends the ticket text to an AI provider and stores the returned summary — one request, one response, no further AI-driven decisions

A travel-booking tool that is told "find me the cheapest three-stop route to Lisbon under $600" and then searches multiple sites, compares results, and books the one that fits — deciding its own next step at each stage

hints: The line between API call and agent isn't "does it use an API" — both do. It's whether one request produces one answer, or whether the system keeps deciding what to do next on its own.
Embedded features are recognisable by having no visible AI interface at all — the AI is doing something inside a tool built for another purpose.
explanation: The support ticket summariser is a plain API call: one piece of text goes in, one summary comes back, and nothing about the system decides its own next move — a person or a fixed program handles what happens after. The travel tool is an agent precisely because it doesn't stop after one exchange: it searches, evaluates what it found, and chooses to act again based on that, repeatedly, with less human input at each individual step. That escalation — from single-shot API call to multi-step agent — is also where things get harder to predict and audit, which lesson three and four come back to.

prompt: A developer tells a non-technical client: "we'll call the API to generate the product descriptions." What is actually happening when that code runs?

options.text: The code downloads a copy of the AI model and runs it on the client's own computer
The code sends a text request over the internet to the provider's server, which sends back a text response
The code opens a chat window automatically and someone still has to type into it
The code installs a plugin into the client's website that talks to the AI on its own schedule

hints: Nothing is being downloaded or installed on anyone's machine.
Think of it like posting a letter and getting a reply, except it takes about a second and happens over the internet automatically.
explanation: An API call is a request sent over the internet — text in, text back — to a server the provider runs, not a program installed locally and not a chat window with a human in the loop. The model itself, all the enormous computing power behind it, stays on the provider's servers; your code just sends it a message and waits for a reply, the same way a web browser sends a request to a website and gets a page back. That's also why it needs an internet connection and stops working the moment that connection, or the provider's service, is unavailable — a real limit lesson five in this phase touches on.

prompt: Statement: "Once a company builds a feature that calls an AI API, it never has to think about that dependency again — it's a one-time setup, like installing software."

config.statement: Once a company builds a feature that calls an AI API, it never has to think about that dependency again — it's a one-time setup, like installing software.
config.rubric: A strong answer names at least one ongoing dependency: the provider can change prices, change or retire a model version, have outages, or change how a prompt needs to be worded — none of which the company controls once it's live.

hints: Installing software runs entirely on your own machine afterward. An API call needs the provider's server to be up, every single time.
What happens to the feature if the provider raises prices, or retires the exact model version the code was written against?
explanation: False, and by a wide margin. Every single time that feature runs, it depends on the provider's server being reachable, the account still having valid billing, the specific model version still existing (providers do retire older models), and the exact wording of the prompt still producing the expected shape of response — providers do sometimes change how a model responds to the same prompt when they update it. "Set it up once" describes writing the code; it does not describe the ongoing dependency the code creates, which needs monitoring the same way any other live, internet-connected part of a product does.

prompt: A no-code automation (built in a tool like Zapier or Make) is set up: when a new form response arrives, send it to an AI provider, then post the AI's reply to a Slack channel. It works perfectly in testing with five sample responses. In week two, a form response arrives with an unusual field — a customer pastes in three paragraphs where a one-line answer was expected — and the automation posts a garbled, half-cut-off reply to Slack. What does this expose about no-code AI tools generally?

options.text: No-code tools are unreliable and shouldn't be used for anything real
Testing with a handful of tidy examples doesn't reveal how a workflow handles messy, unexpected real input
The AI provider's model was faulty that week

hints: Five sample responses were probably all well-formed. Real customers are not always well-formed.
This isn't really about no-code specifically — it's about the gap between a demo and production traffic, which no-code tools make especially easy to skip past.
explanation: The honest lesson isn't "no-code is unreliable" — it's that no-code tools make it very easy to build something that works beautifully on the tidy examples you tested and to skip the step of asking "what happens with input nobody planned for." That gap exists in coded systems too, but no-code tools' visual, drag-and-drop simplicity often gives a false sense that the hard part (handling edge cases) is done, when actually only the happy path was ever tested. The fix isn't abandoning no-code — it's deliberately testing with a messy, unexpected input before trusting a workflow with real customers.

prompt: Name a real, recurring task in your own work or life that you'd consider handing to a no-code AI workflow. Describe the single messiest, most unexpected version of the input it would need to survive before you'd actually trust it.
hints: Think about the input that would arrive on the worst day, not the average day.
"Messiest" usually means: longest, most ambiguous, missing a field, or written by someone in a hurry or upset.
explanation: There's no single right answer here — the point is the specificity. A workflow that routes customer emails needs to survive the customer who writes four paragraphs of context before asking their actual question; a workflow that categorises expenses needs to survive a transaction description that's just a person's name with no other detail. Naming the actual worst-case input for your actual task is what turns "test it first" from advice into something you'll really do.

prompt: A friend says: "No-code AI tools are basically the same as hiring a developer, just free and instant." Name two specific ways that's wrong — not "it's more complicated than that" in general, but two concrete differences a person would actually run into.
hints: Think about what happens when something breaks at 2am, or when the workflow needs to do something the tool's building blocks genuinely can't do.
Think about cost too — "free" undersells what these tools actually charge for at real volume.
explanation: Two concrete differences: first, when something breaks or produces a wrong result, a developer can read the actual code and reason about exactly why, while a no-code workflow's failure often shows up as a vague error in a visual log with no way to see what request was actually sent or why it produced that output — debugging is harder, not easier, once something goes wrong in an unusual way. Second, "free" is misleading at real volume: most no-code platforms charge per workflow run or per "task" above a low free tier, and that cost stacks with whatever the AI provider itself charges per request, so a workflow that felt free in testing can get expensive fast once it's actually handling hundreds of real form submissions a month. Neither of these means no-code tools are bad — it means they trade some of a developer's flexibility and debuggability for speed and low upfront cost, which is a real trade, not a strictly better deal.

prompt: Put these steps in the order you'd actually go through when deciding whether a repeated chat-window task is worth turning into a script or automation instead.

items: Notice you've typed a near-identical prompt into a chat window more than a handful of times
Check whether the output needs to be identically formatted every time, or whether variation is fine
Estimate how often this will keep happening over the next few months
Weigh the setup effort (or cost of paying someone) against the time it will actually save
Decide: keep doing it by hand, or invest in a script/automation

hints: The trigger for even considering automation is noticing repetition — that always comes first.
Setup cost only makes sense to weigh once you know how often the task recurs and how strict the output needs to be.
explanation: Repetition is the signal that starts the conversation, but it isn't sufficient on its own — a task you do rarely, or one where the output can vary freely each time, often isn't worth automating even if it recurs. The order matters because each step narrows the decision: noticing repetition tells you it's worth looking at, checking format consistency tells you whether a fixed script can even do the job reliably, estimating future frequency tells you whether the investment will pay off, and only then does weighing setup cost against time saved produce a real answer rather than a guess.

prompt: Match each situation to whether a script/automation or a manual chat conversation genuinely fits it better.

pairs.left: Reformatting the same weekly sales report into the same fixed template, every Monday, for eight months running
Brainstorming five possible taglines for a one-off product launch, refining based on gut reaction as you go
Drafting a personalised reply to each of 200 nearly-identical customer emails asking about the same delayed shipment
Working through a genuinely novel, one-time strategic decision where you want to think out loud and push back on the AI's suggestions

hints: Repetition with a fixed shape favours scripting. Genuine back-and-forth thinking, done once, favours chat.
200 near-identical emails is exactly the volume where typing the same prompt 200 times stops making sense.
explanation: The pattern across all four: scripting wins when the task repeats with a consistent shape and doesn't need a human's judgement mid-task — the weekly report and the 200 shipment replies both fit that. Manual chat wins when the value is in the back-and-forth itself — brainstorming a tagline or working through a novel decision benefits from you steering, reacting, and changing direction, which a fixed script can't do and shouldn't try to.

prompt: A solo consultant wants help triaging the 15-20 emails she gets a week so the urgent ones surface first. A friend suggests building a multi-step agent that reads each email, checks her calendar, checks a client database, and decides priority and drafts replies autonomously. What's the strongest argument for starting with something much simpler first?

options.text: Agents are always a bad idea and should be avoided entirely

At 15-20 emails a week, a much simpler pattern (even just asking a chat tool to triage a daily batch, or a basic API-driven priority-flag) can likely do the whole job, and is far easier to verify is working correctly
Agents can only be built by large companies with engineering teams

hints: The question isn't whether an agent *could* do this — it's whether the task's actual size and complexity need that much machinery.
A simpler system is also a system you can fully understand and check, which matters a lot when it's touching your actual client relationships.
explanation: The strongest argument isn't that agents are bad — it's proportionality. Fifteen to twenty emails a week is a small, low-complexity volume, and a much simpler approach (a daily chat session where she pastes in the batch and asks for a priority ranking, or a simple script that flags keywords and sends her a daily digest) is very likely to do the whole job just as well, while being something she can fully see and verify, rather than a multi-step system making autonomous decisions about client communication that she'd need to trust without being able to watch each step. The pattern to build gets more sophisticated only when the simpler one demonstrably can't keep up — not before.

prompt: For each pair, sort which option is "the simplest thing that works" for the situation described, versus which is over-engineered for it.

items.text: A solo photographer manually asking a chat tool to write 5 Instagram captions once a week
The same photographer building a multi-tool autonomous agent to research trends, generate captions, and auto-post them, for 5 captions a week
A 40-person company building an automated API pipeline to draft the ~300 personalised order-confirmation emails it sends daily
That same 40-person company having a staff member manually chat-prompt all 300 confirmations by hand every day

hints: "Over-engineered" doesn't only mean "too much automation" — it can also mean "too much manual effort for a volume that clearly needs automating."
Match the machinery to the actual volume and complexity, in both directions.
explanation: The pairing is deliberate: over-engineering runs both ways. Building an autonomous multi-tool agent for five weekly captions is far more machinery than the task needs — a two-minute chat session does it. But having a person manually type 300 near-identical prompts a day is the opposite mistake: too much manual effort for a volume that plainly calls for an automated pipeline. "Simplest thing that works" is relative to the actual size of the job, not a rule that always means "do less."

prompt: A freelance illustrator wants help, once, deciding what order to display 12 portfolio pieces in for a specific client pitch — a judgement call she wants to think through interactively, not repeat. Which pattern fits?

options.text: Chat interface
A custom API-driven script
A multi-step agent

hints: One-off, needs her judgement and reaction at each step — that's the profile chat fits.
explanation: Chat: a one-off, judgement-heavy task where she wants to think out loud and react is exactly what conversational back-and-forth is for. Building a script or agent for something that happens once and needs her steering throughout would cost more setup effort than the task could ever save.

prompt: Sort each task by the pattern that actually fits it best.

items.text: A photographer manually asking for 5 caption ideas before a single post
A dental clinic's booking software auto-drafting appointment reminder texts with no visible prompt anywhere
A newsletter tool that, every Monday at 9am, pulls the week's blog posts and generates a fixed-format digest email automatically
A research tool given "compile everything published on this topic in the last year" that searches, filters, and decides what's relevant across multiple passes

hints: Fixed trigger, fixed output shape, no visible chat = script. Deciding its own next step across multiple passes = agent.
explanation: The newsletter digest is a script: a fixed schedule, a fixed format, one request each Monday, no self-directed decision-making. The research tool is an agent precisely because "everything published" isn't a single request — it requires searching, evaluating what came back, and deciding whether to search again, repeatedly.

prompt: A charity gets the same three-paragraph donor thank-you email question every week from a volunteer coordinator. Order the steps that lead to a sound decision about automating it.

items: Notice the same request keeps coming from the same person, weekly
Check whether every thank-you needs the same structure, or whether each donor's note genuinely differs
If the structure is fixed, test a script against a deliberately unusual donor record before trusting it
Decide to automate or keep it manual based on what the test showed

hints: Recognising repetition comes first, but it's structure — not just frequency — that decides whether automation is safe.
explanation: This mirrors lesson four directly: repetition alone (step 1) isn't the decision, checking whether the *shape* stays consistent (step 2) is, and even once that looks true, testing against an unusual case (step 3) before trusting it with real donor communication is what separates a safe automation from a Tuesday-shaped surprise.

prompt: Statement: "A no-code AI workflow that works correctly on every example you tested it with is ready for real, unattended use."

config.statement: A no-code AI workflow that works correctly on every example you tested it with is ready for real, unattended use.
config.rubric: A strong answer names that passing chosen test examples only proves the wiring works, not that it will handle input nobody thought to test, especially messy or unexpected real-world cases.

hints: What kind of examples did you choose to test with — and who chose them?
explanation: False. Passing every example you thought to test only proves the workflow handles the cases you imagined — it says nothing about the messy, unexpected input real use will eventually produce. The lesson's squash-or-weed report and the water-heater leak are both examples of exactly this gap: tidy test data hiding a real failure mode.

prompt: Match each scenario to whether it's right-sized or over-engineered for its actual volume and complexity.

pairs.left: A 3-person shop building a full autonomous agent to handle its ~8 weekly customer emails
A national retailer with 40,000 daily orders using a coded API pipeline to draft order confirmations
A student manually chat-drafting a single scholarship essay once
A 500-person call centre having agents manually type the same AI prompt for each of 3,000 daily calls

right: Cannot be assessed without more information

hints: Over-engineering runs in both directions — too much automation for a tiny task, and too little for a huge one.
explanation: The pairing deliberately runs both ways: an agent for 8 weekly emails is far more machinery than the volume needs, while 3,000 daily manual prompts at a call centre is the opposite failure — a volume that plainly calls for automation being handled by hand.

prompt: Think of a task you personally do at least weekly that involves typing something similar into an AI chat tool each time. Using this module's tests — repetition, fixed shape, whether judgement varies — decide honestly whether it's a script/automation candidate, and say what specifically would need to stay identical each time for that to work.
hints: Be specific about what part is genuinely identical each time and what part actually varies.
If you can't name a task like this, describe the closest one — most people have at least a near-miss.
explanation: There's no fixed right answer; what matters is applying the test honestly rather than reaching for whichever conclusion sounds better. A task genuinely qualifies when both the trigger and the required output shape repeat consistently — if you notice the output actually needs to vary meaningfully each time (different tone for different recipients, different depth depending on context), that's a sign it should stay manual, or move to a script only for the parts that are genuinely fixed.

prompt: A nonprofit is deciding how to handle grant application status updates to 60 applicants. Updates happen twice a year, in batches, with mostly the same three outcomes (accepted / declined / waitlisted) but declined applicants sometimes need a genuinely individual paragraph of feedback if a reviewer wrote detailed notes. What's the most defensible approach?

options.text: A single script that sends all 60 with a fixed template based on outcome, no exceptions
A script for the fixed-template accepted/waitlisted batches, combined with manual chat-assisted drafting for declined applicants who have reviewer notes
A full autonomous agent that reads reviewer notes and decides tone and content for all 60 with no review

hints: The task isn't uniform — most of it is fixed-shape, but part of it genuinely needs individual judgement. What does that suggest about splitting the approach?
Twice a year, batched, is low enough volume that even the manual part is very manageable.
explanation: This scenario deliberately doesn't have a single clean answer, because the task isn't uniform: the accepted and waitlisted outcomes are genuinely fixed-shape and fit a script well, while declined applicants with detailed reviewer notes need real, individual judgement a fixed template would flatten. Splitting the approach — script for the part that's actually fixed, manual chat-assisted drafting for the part that genuinely varies — respects what each part of the task actually needs, rather than forcing one pattern onto all of it. A full unreviewed agent handling feedback that will land emotionally with a real rejected applicant is the highest-risk option here, for a task that doesn't need that much autonomy.

prompt: A freelance video editor spends about 45 minutes every single week manually renaming, sorting into folders, and logging incoming client footage before she can start editing. She's never thought of this as "automatable" because it doesn't feel like AI work — it feels like admin. Is she right to rule it out?

options.text: Yes — automation is for AI-flavoured tasks like writing or summarising, not file admin
No — a task that repeats weekly, has a clear trigger (footage arrives) and a consistent shape (rename, sort, log) is exactly the profile worth automating, whether or not it involves writing
No, but only if she learns to code first

hints: What made this a candidate isn't whether it's "AI-flavoured" — it's whether it repeats predictably.
Nothing about the earlier module said automation candidates have to involve generating text.
explanation: She's ruling it out for the wrong reason. "Automatable" isn't about whether a task feels like writing or summarising — it's about whether it repeats on a recognisable trigger with a consistent shape, which file renaming and sorting clearly does. An AI step might not even be the main event here (renaming by a pattern is pure rule-following); AI's specific value might be reading footage filenames or a shoot log to guess sensible folder names automatically — a small but real judgement call inside an otherwise mechanical task.

prompt: List three tasks you personally repeat at least monthly. For each, name the trigger (what starts it) and roughly how much time it costs per occurrence. Then say which one is the strongest automation candidate and why — using the trigger and consistency of shape, not just "it's annoying."
hints: A trigger is the specific thing that starts the task — an email arriving, a date on the calendar, a form being submitted. "I feel like it's time" isn't a trigger.
The strongest candidate usually has both a clear trigger and a consistent output shape — not just high annoyance.
explanation: There's no single correct list, but the reasoning should isolate trigger clarity and shape consistency as the actual deciding factors, not just which task is most irritating. A task with a vague or inconsistent trigger ("whenever I feel behind on filing") is much harder to automate reliably than one with a sharp trigger ("every Monday at 9am" or "whenever an email arrives from this specific sender"), even if the vague one feels more urgent day to day.

prompt: A community centre wants to automate: when someone signs up for a workshop via a form, send them a personalised welcome email that mentions which workshop they picked and one thing to bring. Put the pieces in the order a no-code automation actually wires them.

items: Trigger: new form submission received
Action: send the submission's workshop name and any notes to an AI step, asking for a short personalised welcome paragraph
Action: insert that paragraph into the email template
Action: send the completed email to the address from the form

hints: A no-code automation always starts with exactly one trigger, then runs through a fixed sequence of actions.
The AI step here is one action among several, not the whole automation.
explanation: Every no-code automation has this same skeleton: one trigger that starts it, then a sequence of actions. The AI step isn't special in the wiring — it's just one action in the chain, taking the workshop name and notes as input and producing a paragraph as output, which the next action then uses. Getting the order right matters because each action typically needs the previous one's output.

prompt: In no-code automation platforms, what's the difference between a "trigger" and an "action"?

options.text: A trigger is the one event that starts the automation running; actions are the steps that happen afterward, in order
A trigger is any step that uses AI; an action is any step that doesn't
There's no real difference — both terms describe the same thing

hints: Every automation has exactly one trigger and can have many actions.
AI can appear in an action, but "trigger" and "action" describe timing and role, not whether AI is involved.
explanation: A trigger is the single event that kicks the whole thing off — a new form response, an email arriving, a scheduled time. Actions are everything that happens next, run in sequence, and there can be several of them — sending data to an AI step, writing to a spreadsheet, posting a message. An AI step is simply one possible kind of action, not a separate category from trigger and action.

prompt: A support team's automation: whenever a customer email arrives, immediately send it to an AI step to draft a reply, then send that reply automatically. Two weeks in, a customer who'd already been replied to manually by a teammate an hour earlier gets a second, AI-drafted reply saying something slightly different. What does this expose about where the AI step was placed?

options.text: The AI step should come first in the chain, always
The chain was missing a check — before drafting a reply, it needed to verify the email hadn't already been handled — placed before the AI step, not after
AI shouldn't draft customer replies at all

hints: The problem isn't the AI step itself — it's what was missing *before* it.
A dedupe or status check is a deterministic, rule-based step — exactly the kind that belongs before a judgement-requiring AI step, not folded into it.
explanation: The AI step drafting a reply isn't the flaw — the flaw is that nothing checked, before reaching that step, whether the email had already been handled. That's a simple, rule-based check (has this thread already gotten a reply?) that belongs earlier in the chain, filtering out cases the AI step should never see. Placing deterministic checks before the judgement-requiring AI step, rather than folding everything into one "AI does it all" step, is exactly what lesson three is about.

prompt: In a job-application screening automation, the AI step is placed first: every incoming résumé goes straight to an AI step that decides pass/fail before any other check happens. Name one deterministic check that should probably happen *before* the AI step, and explain what problem placing it first would prevent.
hints: A deterministic check is something a simple rule can decide, no judgement needed — a required field being present, a duplicate submission, a basic eligibility fact.
What happens if the same résumé gets submitted twice and both went straight to the (possibly inconsistent) AI step?
explanation: A strong answer names something like: checking that all required fields are actually present (so the AI step isn't asked to judge an incomplete application as though it were a real one), or checking for duplicate submissions from the same applicant (so the same person isn't scored twice with possibly different results each time, since AI outputs aren't perfectly identical run to run). Placing either check before the AI step means the AI step only ever sees applications worth judging, rather than spending its one, harder-to-audit judgement on cases a simple rule could have already resolved.

prompt: An automation processes 200 incoming supplier invoices a week, sending each to an AI step to extract the amount and due date. One week, the AI provider has a brief outage and 40 of the 200 requests fail silently — the automation just moves on without those 40 rows. Nobody notices for a month, and three supplier payments are missed. What was actually missing from this automation?

options.text: A faster AI provider
Any failure handling at all — a way to notice, log, or flag when a step doesn't complete, rather than silently continuing
Human involvement in every single invoice, defeating the point of automating

hints: The AI provider having an outage is going to happen occasionally, from any provider — the real design question is what the automation does when that happens.
Notice this isn't asking for full manual review of everything — just something that flags when a step didn't complete.
explanation: Outages happen; that's not a design flaw on its own. The actual missing piece is failure handling — anything that would have noticed 40 requests failed and done something about it, even something as simple as a log entry and a weekly "failed items" notification. Without that, a silent failure is indistinguishable from success until the real-world consequence (missed payments) surfaces weeks later. Full manual review of every invoice would defeat the point of automating — the fix isn't watching everything, it's making failures visible instead of silent.

prompt: Put these steps in the order you'd actually go through when adding failure handling to an existing automation.

items: List the specific points in the chain where a step could fail (AI request times out, required field missing, output doesn't match expected format)
For each failure point, decide what should happen instead of silently continuing — retry, flag to a human, or log and skip
Add a way to be notified when a failure actually occurs, rather than having to check logs constantly
Deliberately trigger each failure type once, on purpose, to confirm the handling actually works

hints: You can't design a response to a failure you haven't identified yet — naming the failure points comes first.
Testing that failure handling actually works is the step people skip most often.
explanation: Each step depends on the one before it: you can't decide a response without first naming the specific ways a step can fail, you can't get useful notifications without first deciding what counts as a failure worth flagging, and none of it is trustworthy until you've deliberately broken it once to confirm the handling actually triggers — which is the step most commonly skipped, leaving failure handling that looks complete but has never actually fired.

prompt: Statement: "An automation that you check manually every single day, just in case, is functioning as intended."

config.statement: An automation that you check manually every single day, just in case, is functioning as intended.
config.rubric: A strong answer notes that daily manual checking, done indefinitely because you don't trust it, is supervised manual work with extra steps — not automation that's actually earned trust.

hints: What was the whole point of building the automation in the first place?
There's a real difference between an occasional spot-check and checking every single day out of low-level worry.
explanation: False. If an automation still needs a human checking its output every day, indefinitely, the automation hasn't actually removed the manual work — it's added a layer on top of it while still requiring the same daily attention. Genuine automation success looks like trustworthy failure handling (lesson four) plus occasional, spaced spot-checks, not daily vigilance that never ends.

prompt: Describe a real automation you have, or one you're planning from this module's lab, and name specifically what would let you stop checking it every day. Be concrete — not "I'd trust it more," but what exact signal or safeguard would earn that trust.
hints: A concrete answer names something checkable: a notification that only fires on failure, a weekly summary instead of daily checking, a specific number of clean runs before you relax.
"I'd just trust it eventually" isn't a mechanism — what would actually have to be true?
explanation: A strong answer names a specific mechanism, not a feeling — something like: "once failure notifications only arrive when something actually breaks, instead of me checking a log daily, I'd move to a weekly spot-check instead," or "after two weeks of clean runs with the failure handling from lesson four in place, I'd trust the fallback path enough to stop watching it daily." The shift from daily babysitting to occasional spot-checking has to be earned by something concrete and checkable — not just time passing.

prompt: A hairdresser gets asked "do you have any openings this week" by DM roughly 15 times a week, always answerable from her existing booking calendar. Is this an automation candidate by this module's test?

options.text: Yes — clear trigger (a DM arrives with this question), real recurring cost, consistent shape (check calendar, reply with openings)
No — it involves a real human conversation, so it can't be automated
No — 15 times a week isn't enough repetition to matter

hints: Check it against all three conditions from lesson one, not just one of them.
15 times a week, at even a minute or two each, adds up over a year.
explanation: Yes, by all three conditions: a clear trigger (an incoming DM asking about openings), real recurring cost (15/week adds up fast), and a consistent shape (check the same calendar, answer the same kind of question). "Involves conversation" doesn't disqualify it — an automated reply checking her calendar and drafting a natural response handles exactly this shape well.

prompt: A vet clinic wants: when a new appointment is booked, check if the pet has any flagged allergies on file, and only then have AI draft a pre-visit reminder mentioning relevant care notes. Order the chain.

items: Trigger: new appointment booked
Action: look up the pet's record for flagged allergies or notes
Action: send the appointment details and any flagged notes to an AI step for a personalised reminder
Action: send the reminder to the owner

hints: The deterministic lookup (checking flagged notes) belongs before the AI step, feeding it what it needs to reference.
explanation: The record lookup is deterministic — a simple data check — and belongs before the AI step so the AI step has the right information to reference, rather than guessing or omitting it. This mirrors lesson three: rule-based steps first, AI step exactly where judgement (turning notes into a natural reminder) is actually needed.

prompt: For a job-application automation, sort each check by whether it belongs before the AI step (deterministic) or is the kind of thing the AI step itself should handle (judgement).

items.text: Confirming all required fields were filled in
Checking this isn't a duplicate submission from the same applicant
Summarising how a candidate's stated experience relates to the role's requirements
Drafting a personalised note about which parts of the application stood out

hints: A deterministic check is answerable by a fixed rule with no interpretation needed. Judgement tasks need reading and interpreting varied text.
explanation: Required-field and duplicate checks are answerable by a fixed rule with no interpretation — exactly what belongs before the AI step. Relating varied, free-text experience to a role, or drafting a note about what stood out, both require reading and interpreting — the genuine judgement an AI step is for.

prompt: Statement: "If an automation hasn't failed yet, its failure handling is probably fine."

config.statement: If an automation hasn't failed yet, its failure handling is probably fine.
config.rubric: A strong answer notes that failure handling that has never actually been triggered (deliberately or otherwise) hasn't been demonstrated to work — absence of failure so far isn't the same as tested failure handling.

hints: Has the failure handling ever actually been triggered and observed to work, or has it just never been needed yet?
explanation: False. Not having failed yet says nothing about whether the failure handling would actually work if it were needed — it might be broken and simply never tested. Lesson four's sequencing exercise specifically ends with deliberately triggering each failure type once, which is the only way to know the handling works rather than hoping it does.

prompt: Match each automation situation to the failure-handling response that actually fits it.

pairs.left: An AI step occasionally times out under normal load
An AI step returns an oddly formatted result that doesn't match the expected shape
pairs.right: Log it and flag for human review rather than sending it on

pairs.left: A whole batch fails because the provider is down for an hour
pairs.right: Queue and retry the batch later, with a notification if it's still failing after a set time

right: Silently skip and continue with no record

hints: Match the response to what actually caused the failure — a transient timeout differs from a malformed result differs from a provider outage.
explanation: A brief timeout under normal load often resolves on a simple retry. A malformed result is a signal something's actually wrong with that specific case and needs a human's eyes before it goes anywhere, not a retry. A provider-wide outage needs queuing and patience, plus an escalating notification if it drags on — three different failures, three different sound responses, none of which is "say nothing and move on."

prompt: Describe an automation (yours or hypothetical) that would currently need daily checking. Name the one specific change to its failure handling or notifications that would let you check it weekly instead.
hints: Be specific about the mechanism — a notification, a spot-check schedule, a demonstrated track record — not just "trust it more."
What exactly would have to be true for weekly to feel safe instead of reckless?
explanation: A strong answer names a concrete mechanism: a failure-only notification replacing daily full review, or a demonstrated two-week track record against deliberately triggered failures, matching lesson five's synthesis. A vague "I'd just get used to it" answer misses the point — the shift to less frequent checking needs to be earned by something checkable, not by habituation.

prompt: A florist's automation drafts personalised delivery-day messages for corporate clients, pulling from an order form. One order form response has an empty "occasion" field because the customer skipped it. What should happen?

options.text: The AI step should guess a plausible occasion and proceed as normal
A deterministic check before the AI step should catch the missing required field and flag it for a human, rather than letting the AI step guess
The whole automation should be scrapped since one field was empty

hints: Guessing a missing fact and presenting it confidently is a specific risk this module and the previous one both name — what's the safer alternative?
One malformed input doesn't mean the automation is broken — it means this case needs a different path.
explanation: Letting the AI step guess an occasion it wasn't actually told invites a confidently wrong message going out to a real client — exactly the kind of thing a deterministic pre-check should catch first. Flagging the missing field for a human to fill in or confirm keeps the automation running for every well-formed case while routing the genuinely incomplete one somewhere safer than a guess.

prompt: A hobbyist builds a weekend project — a chatbot that summarises news articles — expecting it to be roughly free, since a chat subscription he already pays for feels unlimited. He wires it to an API instead of the subscription, tests it against 200 long articles over the weekend, and gets a $34 bill. What's the most accurate explanation?

options.text: API billing charges per unit of text processed — both what you send in and what comes back — regardless of any separate subscription he pays for elsewhere
The API provider made a billing error, since AI usage is normally free
His chat subscription should have covered this automatically

hints: A chat subscription and an API account are separate things, billed separately, even from the same provider.
200 long articles, both sent in and summarised back out, is a real volume of text — it isn't free to process.
explanation: API usage is billed per unit of text (tokens) processed — both the text sent in (the article) and the text generated back (the summary) — and that billing is completely separate from any consumer chat subscription, which covers a different product entirely. Two hundred long articles, each contributing thousands of input tokens and a meaningful number of output tokens, adds up to a real, billable volume — the surprise wasn't a billing error, it was not distinguishing "I pay for chat" from "the API I wired my project into bills separately, per use."

prompt: In plain terms, without using the word "token" more than once, explain to someone non-technical why a longer document costs more to summarise via an API than a short paragraph does.
hints: Think about what's actually being measured and charged — the length of the text going in, and the length of what comes back.
Avoid "it just does" — name the actual mechanism: more text in, more units of text processed, more cost.
explanation: A workable explanation: the AI provider charges based on roughly how much text is processed on each request, both what you send it and what it writes back — so a ten-page document costs meaningfully more to summarise than a two-sentence one, the same way a print shop would charge more to photocopy ten pages than two, even though both are "just copying." The exact billing unit is a chunk of text (a fraction of a word, on average), but the plain-language version — length in, length out, both counted — is enough to reason about cost without memorising the mechanics.

prompt: Before building the support-email automation from module two, its designer wants to estimate monthly cost. She knows: roughly 2,000 emails a month, each email averages about 300 input tokens (the email plus instructions) and 150 output tokens (the drafted reply), and the model costs (hypothetically) $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens. What's the right way to combine these?

options.text: (300 + 150) × $3/million, once, since it's the same model

hints: Input and output are priced differently and need to be calculated separately, then added together.
The volume (2,000 emails) multiplies each part, not the combined per-token price.
explanation: Input tokens and output tokens are billed at different rates, so each needs its own calculation — total input tokens (2,000 × 300) times the input price, plus total output tokens (2,000 × 150) times the output price — before adding the two together. That works out to (600,000 × $3/million) + (300,000 × $15/million) = $1.80 + $4.50 = $6.30 a month for this volume — cheap enough here to matter less than it might at higher volume, which is exactly why doing the estimate first, before assuming, is worth the five minutes.

prompt: Using the same style of estimate as the exercise above, roughly cost out an automation of your own (real or from this phase's earlier labs): estimate monthly volume, average input and output tokens per use, and multiply through with any current per-token price you can find or estimate. Show your work, including which numbers you're genuinely unsure about.
hints: It's fine to use round, honestly-labelled guesses for token counts if you don't have exact ones — the point is doing the multiplication, not achieving false precision.
Separate input and output token estimates, since they're usually priced differently.
explanation: There's no single correct number here — what matters is the structure: a volume estimate, a per-use input token estimate, a per-use output token estimate, current (or reasonably estimated) per-token prices for both, calculated separately and added together, with genuine uncertainty flagged rather than hidden behind false precision. An estimate that says "roughly $8-15/month depending on average email length, which I'm not fully sure of" is more honest and more useful than a single confident number built on a guess presented as a fact.

prompt: A small business already pays $20/month for an individual's AI chat subscription. They want to add an automation that drafts 2,000 order-confirmation emails a month, and someone suggests "we already pay for AI, just use that." Why doesn't that work?

options.text: Consumer chat subscriptions are for one person chatting in a browser or app — they don't provide the API access an automated, code-driven workflow needs to run unattended
Subscriptions are always more expensive than usage billing, so it's a bad financial choice
It would work fine — a subscription covers unlimited use of the AI, however it's accessed

hints: What does a $20/month chat subscription actually grant access to — a chat interface, or a programmable API?
Whether it's cheaper isn't the issue here — it's whether it's even the right kind of access for an automated workflow.
explanation: A consumer chat subscription grants a person access to a chat interface — it doesn't typically include the programmable API access an automation needs to send requests from code, on a schedule, unattended. Even setting price aside, it's the wrong *kind* of access for this job: usage billing (a separate API account, billed per token) is what a code-driven, unattended workflow actually needs, while the chat subscription remains the right tool for a human's own direct conversations.

prompt: Statement: "Usage billing is always cheaper than a subscription, so anyone serious about cost should switch to usage billing."

config.statement: Usage billing is always cheaper than a subscription, so anyone serious about cost should switch to usage billing.
config.rubric: A strong answer notes that a subscription's fixed price can beat usage billing for someone who uses AI heavily and steadily, while usage billing suits variable or automated workloads — which is cheaper depends on the actual usage pattern, not a universal rule.

hints: Think about someone who chats with an AI tool for hours every single day — would a per-token bill for that usage necessarily be cheaper than a flat $20?
"Always cheaper" is a strong claim — does it hold for every usage pattern, or just some?
explanation: False. Someone using an AI chat tool heavily and steadily every day might genuinely spend more under usage billing than a flat subscription fee — that's exactly the profile subscriptions are priced for. Usage billing tends to win for variable, automated, or occasional workloads (an automation that runs 2,000 times one month and 200 the next), where a fixed subscription fee would either be wasted in slow months or insufficient in busy ones. Which is cheaper is a question about the actual usage pattern, not a fixed rule in either direction.

prompt: An automation classifies incoming support tickets into one of four fixed categories (billing, technical, shipping, other) — a simple judgement call — using the most expensive, most capable model a provider offers, because "why not use the best one." What's the issue?

options.text: The most capable model is being paid for on a task that a much cheaper, smaller model would very likely handle just as reliably, since simple fixed-category classification doesn't need top-tier reasoning
There's no issue — more capable models are always the right choice
Cheaper models can never be trusted for anything

hints: What does four-category classification actually require — deep reasoning, or a simpler kind of judgement?
"Why not use the best one" ignores that better usually costs meaningfully more per token, for a task that may not need the difference.
explanation: Classifying into a small, fixed set of categories is a comparatively simple judgement — the kind smaller, cheaper models are generally quite reliable at — while top-tier models earn their higher price on much harder tasks: nuanced reasoning, long-context synthesis, creative or ambiguous writing. Paying premium per-token prices for every single ticket, at whatever the ticket volume is, when a cheaper model would likely classify just as accurately, is real money spent on capability the task doesn't need — the same "simplest thing that works" principle from module one, applied to model choice instead of pattern choice.

prompt: Sort each task by whether it's a good fit for a cheaper, smaller model or genuinely needs a more capable (and pricier) one.

categories: Probably needs a more capable model

items.text: Classifying a support ticket into one of four fixed categories
Extracting a date and dollar amount from a standardised invoice format
Drafting a nuanced, persuasive grant proposal synthesising a 40-page research report
items.category: Probably needs a more capable model

items.text: Debugging a subtle, multi-step logical inconsistency across a long legal contract
items.category: Probably needs a more capable model

hints: Fixed-category classification and simple structured extraction are usually low-complexity judgement calls. Synthesis across long, nuanced material and multi-step reasoning are not.
explanation: Fixed-category classification and pulling a date/amount from a standard format are narrow, well-defined judgement calls — the profile cheaper models handle reliably. Synthesising a 40-page report into persuasive writing, or tracing a subtle multi-step inconsistency through a long contract, both require sustained reasoning across a lot of context — the profile that justifies paying for a more capable model.

prompt: A student uses a provider's free tier for a semester-long project. Partway through, requests suddenly start failing with an error instead of the usual replies. What's the most useful next question to ask, given the free tier has real limits?

options.text: "Is this a permanent ban, a temporary rate limit, or expired trial credit — and does the error message actually say which?"
"Should I just give up on this provider entirely?"
"Is the whole internet down?"

hints: Free tiers can hit a wall in several genuinely different ways, and the right next step depends on which one this is.
Error messages from AI providers usually say something specific about why a request failed — that's the first place to look.
explanation: Free-tier limits aren't one single thing — a request can fail because of a **rate limit** (too many requests per minute, which usually resolves itself shortly), **expired trial credit** (a one-time allowance that's been used up and needs a paid account to continue), or a **hard monthly cap** (resets on a schedule, or requires upgrading). The error message is usually specific about which, and it changes what to actually do next — waiting a minute is very different from needing to add a payment method.

prompt: Put these in the order that makes sense for planning around free-tier limits on a real project before it matters.

items: Before building, check the specific free tier's limits: rate limit, total credit, and expiry
Estimate whether your project's expected usage will plausibly hit those limits
If it might, decide in advance what happens at the wall — a paid upgrade, a lower-usage fallback, or accepting the project pauses
Build with that decision already made, rather than discovering the wall mid-project

hints: Deciding what happens "at the wall" only makes sense once you know the actual limits and whether your usage will reach them.
explanation: This mirrors lesson four in module two directly: deciding a fallback in advance, before it's needed, is what turns hitting a free-tier wall from a project-stopping surprise into an already-planned-for event. Checking the specific limits first is necessary because free tiers vary a lot between providers — a rate limit, a total credit allowance, and an expiry date are three different kinds of wall, each needing a different plan.

prompt: A workflow processes 500 documents a month, each averaging 800 input tokens and 200 output tokens, at a hypothetical $2/million input and $10/million output. Roughly what's the monthly cost?

options.text: About $1.80
About $18.00
About $0.18

hints: (500 × 800 × $2/million) + (500 × 200 × $10/million) — work each half separately.
explanation: (500 × 800 = 400,000 input tokens × $2/million = $0.80) + (500 × 200 = 100,000 output tokens × $10/million = $1.00) = $1.80 total — a small number at this volume, which is exactly the kind of check worth doing before assuming a workflow is expensive (or cheap) without running the numbers.

prompt: Statement: "Input tokens and output tokens always cost the same per token, so it doesn't matter which side of the request is longer."

config.statement: Input tokens and output tokens always cost the same per token, so it doesn't matter which side of the request is longer.
config.rubric: A strong answer notes output tokens are typically priced higher than input tokens, so a workflow generating long outputs from short inputs costs differently than the reverse.

hints: Which takes more computation: reading existing text, or generating new text?
explanation: False — output tokens are typically priced higher than input tokens, since generating new text takes more computation than processing existing text. A workflow that takes a short instruction and produces a long generated response costs differently, per token processed, than one that takes a long document and produces a short summary — the ratio of input to output length matters, not just the total token count.

prompt: Sort each usage pattern by whether a subscription or usage billing fits it better.

items.text: One person chatting with an AI tool for a couple of hours daily, steadily, for personal writing
An automation that runs 50 times one month and 4,000 the next, depending on business activity
A code-driven workflow that needs to run on a schedule with no person present
A single freelancer's daily, heavy, predictable chat usage for client work

hints: Steady, heavy, individual chat use tends to favour a flat subscription. Variable or code-driven volume tends to favour metered usage billing.
explanation: Steady, predictable, heavy individual chat usage is exactly what a flat subscription is priced around. Widely varying month-to-month volume, and anything code-driven that runs unattended, needs the programmable, metered access usage billing provides — a subscription doesn't offer that kind of access at all, separate from the cost question.

prompt: A workflow extracts a single fixed data field (an order number) from a standardised confirmation email format, at high volume. What's the most cost-sensible model choice?

options.text: A cheaper, smaller model — the task is narrow, structured extraction, not complex reasoning
The most capable model available, to be safe
It doesn't matter — all models cost the same

hints: What kind of judgement does pulling a fixed field from a standardised format actually require?
explanation: Narrow, structured extraction from a consistent format is exactly the profile a cheaper, smaller model handles reliably — paying premium per-token prices for every one of a high volume of simple extractions would be real, avoidable cost for capability the task doesn't need.

prompt: A friend hits a free-tier error mid-project and says "guess the AI just broke." Name the three genuinely different things that could actually be happening, and the one question that would tell them which it is.
hints: Rate limit, expired trial credit, monthly cap — the same three from lesson five.
What does the actual error message say?
explanation: The three possibilities are a rate limit (too many requests too fast, usually temporary), expired trial credit (a one-time allowance used up, needing a paid account), or a monthly cap (a recurring limit that resets on schedule). Reading the actual error message, rather than guessing, is usually the fastest way to tell which — providers are typically specific about which limit was hit, even when the plain-English summary just reads as "it broke."

prompt: A small business wants to estimate whether a planned automation will be affordable before committing to build it. Order the steps.

items: Estimate expected monthly volume
Estimate average input and output tokens per use
Look up (or reasonably estimate) current per-token pricing for input and output
Calculate volume × tokens × price for each side and add them together, labelling any guesses honestly

hints: This is the same shape as lesson two's estimate, applied fresh.
explanation: Each step feeds the next: volume tells you how many times the calculation repeats, token estimates tell you how much each repetition costs to process, pricing turns tokens into money, and only then does the full calculation produce a number worth trusting — with honest labelling of which inputs were genuine guesses.

prompt: A nonprofit is deciding between (a) a $20/month individual chat subscription for one staff member's occasional drafting, and (b) usage billing for an automation that sends about 800 donor-update emails a quarter. What's the most defensible plan?

options.text: Keep the subscription for the staff member's own chat use, and set up separate usage billing for the automation — they're different products for different usage shapes
Cancel the subscription and route everything through usage billing, since it's usually cheaper
Use the $20 subscription to also power the automation, since they already pay for it

hints: A subscription doesn't grant the programmable access an automation needs, regardless of price comparisons.
These are two different needs — an individual's steady chat use and a code-driven quarterly batch job — not one need with two possible prices.
explanation: The subscription and the automation are two different needs entirely, not two price options for the same thing: the staff member's occasional chat drafting is well served by a flat subscription, while the automation needs programmable API access a chat subscription doesn't provide, regardless of whether usage billing turns out cheaper or pricier for that specific quarterly volume. Keeping both, matched to what each actually is, is the defensible plan — not collapsing them into one because it seems simpler.

prompt: Someone asks an AI tool for feedback on their emails roughly three times a week, typing some version of the same request from memory each time — sometimes remembering to ask for a direct tone, sometimes forgetting, sometimes phrasing the "flag anything unclear" part differently. Results vary noticeably. What's actually going wrong?

options.text: The AI is inconsistent and can't be trusted for this kind of task
The prompt itself is being reinvented from memory each time instead of reused, so small wording differences produce genuinely different results
Feedback requests are inherently too unpredictable to ask an AI for

hints: Is the AI actually behaving differently, or is the input changing slightly each time?
"From memory" is doing a lot of work here — what's the alternative to reconstructing a prompt from memory each time?
explanation: The AI isn't the inconsistent part — the input is. A prompt reconstructed from memory each time will vary in exactly the ways this one does: sometimes the tone instruction is there, sometimes it's dropped, sometimes "flag anything unclear" gets phrased slightly differently, and each variation genuinely changes the result. A saved, reused prompt — refined once and kept, rather than reinvented from memory each time — removes that variability entirely.

prompt: Sort each task by whether it's worth a saved prompt library entry, or better left as a one-off, fresh conversation each time.

categories: Fine as a one-off each time

items.text: Asking for direct, kind feedback on a work email draft — something done a few times a week, always wanting the same tone and structure of feedback
A single unusual brainstorm about whether to change careers, unlikely to be repeated in that exact form
items.category: Fine as a one-off each time

items.text: Drafting a weekly status update in the same format, every week, for the same team
Working through a one-time, highly specific negotiation strategy for a single unusual situation
items.category: Fine as a one-off each time

hints: The test is the same shape as module two's automation-candidate test — does this repeat with a consistent enough shape to be worth saving, or is it genuinely one-off?
A library entry doesn't need automation-level repetition — even a few times a week, with a consistent ask, is enough to be worth saving.
explanation: The email feedback and weekly status update both repeat with a consistent shape — exactly what's worth capturing once and reusing, rather than reconstructing from memory each time. The career brainstorm and the one-time negotiation strategy are both genuinely singular — saving a prompt for something that won't recur in that shape again doesn't pay off the way a repeated, consistent ask does.

prompt: A saved library entry reads: "Give me direct but kind feedback on this email draft, flag anything unclear." Each time it's used, the person also has to remember to paste the actual draft in, and remember whether this particular email needs a formal or casual read. What's missing that would make this a proper template rather than just a saved prompt?

options.text: Explicitly marked variable slots — like [DRAFT] and [FORMALITY LEVEL] — so it's obvious what changes each time, instead of relying on memory to fill in the unstated parts
Nothing — a saved prompt and a template are the same thing
The prompt needs to be much longer to become a template

hints: What part of this still relies on the person remembering something, the same problem lesson one was trying to solve?
A template's whole job is to make the changeable parts visible, not just the fixed wording.
explanation: A saved prompt with no marked variable slots still relies on memory for exactly the parts that change — which email to paste, what formality level applies — which is the same failure mode lesson one identified, just moved one level down. A real template names its variable slots explicitly, something like "Give me direct but kind feedback on this email draft: [DRAFT]. Formality level: [FORMAL / CASUAL]. Flag anything unclear," so using it correctly doesn't depend on remembering what to fill in — the template itself asks.

prompt: Take a task you'd save a library entry for (real or from lesson one's exercise). Write it as a proper template: fixed wording plus explicitly marked variable slots, using brackets or a similar clear marker for each thing that changes between uses.
hints: Every part of the prompt that would change between uses needs its own clearly marked slot — don't leave any of it implied.
A good test: could someone else fill in your template correctly without you standing behind them explaining it?
explanation: A strong template names every variable explicitly rather than leaving any of it to memory or inference — something like "Summarise [DOCUMENT] for [AUDIENCE], in [LENGTH] words, focusing on [SPECIFIC ANGLE]." The test in the hint is the real one: if a template only works because the author remembers what each blank is supposed to mean, it hasn't actually solved the problem lesson one raised — it's just moved the memory requirement into a different part of the process.

prompt: On a day when even small decisions feel like too much effort, a full library entry — "Summarise [DOCUMENT] for [AUDIENCE] in [LENGTH] words, focusing on [ANGLE]" — is technically still usable, but something about it is a bad fit for that day specifically. What?

options.text: It still requires deciding audience, length and angle fresh each time — exactly the kind of small decision-making that's hardest on a genuinely low-capacity day
Templates are always too complicated to use on any day
AI tools don't work as well on certain days

hints: What does filling in three separate blanks actually require, cognitively, compared to a version with none left to decide?
The AI's capability isn't changing day to day — what's changing is how much decision-making a person can absorb that day.
explanation: A full template's strength — flexibility across many situations — is exactly what makes it costlier on a day when even ordinary decisions feel heavy: filling in audience, length and angle each requires a small judgement call, and three small judgement calls can be a real ask on a genuinely low-capacity day. A bad-day version of the same entry pre-decides as much as it reasonably can, so using it is closer to "paste and go" than "decide, then paste."

prompt: Match each library entry style to the day it actually fits better.

pairs.right: A normal-capacity day, with attention to spare for a few small decisions

pairs.left: "Summarise this in three plain sentences, for someone with no background on the topic. Paste below."
pairs.right: A low-capacity day, where even small decisions cost more than usual

pairs.left: "Draft a reply matching [TONE], addressing [SPECIFIC POINTS], length [WORD COUNT]"
pairs.right: A normal-capacity day, with attention to spare for a few small decisions

pairs.left: "Draft a short, plain, polite reply to this. Paste below."
pairs.right: A low-capacity day, where even small decisions cost more than usual

hints: The bad-day versions have already made every decision the full versions leave open — tone, length, angle are all pre-set.
explanation: The pattern across both pairs is the same: the full-capacity version leaves useful flexibility open as blanks to fill; the low-capacity version has already made those same decisions in advance, so using it costs almost nothing beyond pasting the content in. Neither version is "better" — they're suited to different days.

prompt: Eight months after building a prompt library, someone notices half their entries reference a project management tool they switched away from three months ago, and a couple of others consistently produce mediocre results they've just gotten used to tolerating. What does this describe?

options.text: A library that's rotted — entries that no longer match reality or quietly stopped earning their place, kept only out of habit
A perfectly healthy library — more entries is always better
A sign the AI model itself has gotten worse over time

hints: "Rotting" doesn't mean the entries were bad when written — it means the world moved and the library didn't.
Tolerating mediocre results out of habit is a specific, nameable failure this lesson is about.
explanation: This is exactly what a rotting library looks like: entries that were genuinely good when written can stop matching reality (referencing a tool that's no longer used) or quietly underperform without anyone questioning why, simply because using them has become habit rather than a deliberate choice. More entries isn't automatically better — an unmaintained pile of stale prompts is worse than a small, actively-used set.

prompt: Statement: "Once a library entry is written and tested, it's finished — there's no ongoing maintenance needed."

config.statement: Once a library entry is written and tested, it's finished — there's no ongoing maintenance needed.
config.rubric: A strong answer notes that circumstances change (tools switch, workflows evolve, models get updated) in ways that can make a previously-good entry stop fitting or stop performing well, without any warning.

hints: Does the world an entry was written for stay the same forever?
This echoes module one lesson two's point about API dependencies never really being finished — is a prompt library any different?
explanation: False, for reasons close to module one's point about API integrations: an entry good enough to save is still built for a specific context — a specific tool, a specific workflow, sometimes a specific model version — and any of those can change quietly. A periodic check (still used? still working? still matches reality?) is what catches an entry that's quietly stopped earning its place before it wastes months of slightly-worse-than-it-should-be results.

prompt: A colleague shares their prompt library as a single long document: thirty prompts, no labels, no notes on when to use which, in the order they happened to be written. What's the actual problem with sharing it this way?

options.text: Nothing — more prompts shared is always more useful
Without labels or context on when to use each one, the receiver has to do all the work of figuring out what each prompt is for before they can use any of them — which defeats the point of sharing
Prompt libraries can't be usefully shared between people with different jobs

hints: What does someone actually need to know before they can use a shared prompt correctly — just the wording, or something more?
"Shared" and "usable by someone else" aren't automatically the same thing.
explanation: Raw wording without context forces the receiver to reverse-engineer what each entry is for, when to reach for it, and what it assumes about their situation — work that can easily cost more than just writing their own prompts from scratch would have. A shareable library needs, for each entry, a short note on what it's for and when to use it — the same information the original author holds in their head but a stranger to the library doesn't.

prompt: Pick two or three entries from your own library (real, or from this module's exercises). Write the one or two sentences of context each would need — what it's for, when to reach for it, what it assumes — for someone who's never seen your work to use it correctly.
hints: What do you know about when to use this entry that isn't written anywhere in the prompt itself?
A good context note answers: what situation is this for, and what does it assume about the reader's own situation?
explanation: There's no fixed correct answer, but a strong context note is specific and short — something like "Use this for external client emails only, not internal team messages; assumes you've already drafted a rough version and want it tightened, not written from scratch." The point is surfacing exactly the unstated knowledge that made the entry usable to its original author but invisible to anyone else.

prompt: Sort each recurring task into whether it's worth a library entry, and if so, whether it needs a full template or a simple saved prompt.

items.text: Asking for a plain-language explanation of any legal clause you paste in, same request every time, no variation needed
Drafting client proposals where audience, tone and length genuinely differ project to project
A single unusual research question you're unlikely to ask again in that form
Weekly team standup notes turned into a summary, same format, same audience, every week

hints: If nothing meaningfully varies between uses, a simple saved prompt is enough — templates earn their extra structure only when real variation exists.
explanation: A task with genuinely fixed wording every time (the legal-clause explainer, weekly standup summary) only needs a saved prompt — building variable slots for nothing that varies adds needless complexity. A task where audience, tone or length genuinely differ each time needs the explicit slots a template provides. A true one-off doesn't earn a spot in the library at all.

prompt: A template reads: "Write a product description for [PRODUCT] in our brand voice." What's the flaw, given the earlier lesson's test?

options.text: "Our brand voice" is not an explicit slot — it depends on the reader already knowing what that means, the same unmarked-memory problem from lesson two
There's no flaw — this is a complete template
Templates should never reference a brand voice

hints: Would someone unfamiliar with "our brand voice" know what to actually write?
explanation: "Our brand voice" is exactly the kind of unmarked variable that lesson two warned about — it reads as fixed wording but actually depends on knowledge the template itself doesn't supply. A complete version would either spell out the brand voice specifically, or make it an explicit slot: [BRAND VOICE: warm, concise, no jargon].

prompt: Statement: "A low-capacity version of a library entry should offer the same range of choices as the full version, just explained more simply."

config.statement: A low-capacity version of a library entry should offer the same range of choices as the full version, just explained more simply.
config.rubric: A strong answer notes the low-capacity version should pre-decide the open choices, not just simplify their explanation — the goal is removing decisions, not making them easier to read.

hints: What's actually costly on a low-capacity day — the number of words explaining a choice, or having to make the choice at all?
explanation: False. Simplifying the *explanation* of a choice still leaves the choice itself to be made, which is the actual cost on a low-capacity day. A genuine low-capacity version pre-decides the open choices (tone, length, angle) in advance, leaving nothing but pasting content in — not a shorter description of the same decisions.

prompt: Someone notices they've manually re-added the same missing instruction to a library entry's output, by hand, for the last six uses in a row. What should this tell them?

options.text: The entry itself needs updating to include that instruction, rather than continuing to patch the output by hand each time
Nothing — occasional manual touch-ups are just part of using AI tools
The AI model needs to be replaced entirely

hints: A repeated manual fix, applied the same way every time, is the specific tell this module names for a rotting entry.
explanation: A single manual touch-up might be nothing. The same fix, applied by hand, six times in a row, is exactly the tell lesson four names — the entry has quietly stopped doing its job, and the fix belongs in the entry itself, not in a habitual manual patch applied after the fact every time.

prompt: Match each library-sharing mistake to what it actually costs the receiver.

pairs.left: Sharing prompts with no notes on when to use each one
pairs.right: The receiver has to reverse-engineer the purpose of every entry before using any of them

pairs.left: Sharing a template whose slots assume software or context the receiver doesn't have
pairs.right: The receiver hits a confusing mismatch they can't resolve without asking the original author

pairs.left: Sharing thirty entries with no organisation at all
pairs.right: The receiver can't quickly find the one entry actually relevant to their task

right: The receiver saves significant time immediately, no downside

hints: Each sharing mistake maps to a specific, real cost for the person receiving it — not a vague "it's not ideal."
explanation: Each mistake has a specific, nameable cost: missing context forces reverse-engineering, unstated assumptions cause confusing mismatches, and no organisation buries the one relevant entry in noise.
