None of these costs disappear just because the sharing act itself was generous — good intentions don't substitute for the context a receiver actually needs.

prompt: Name one entry from your own emerging library (or one from this module's exercises) and write both a full version and a low-capacity version of it, then say in one sentence what's different between them structurally, not just in tone.
hints: The structural difference should be about which decisions are still open versus already made — not just about word count or friendliness.
explanation: The key structural difference to name: the full version leaves genuine choices open as variable slots (tone, length, angle), while the low-capacity version has pre-decided every one of those choices, leaving only the content itself to paste in. A shorter but still choice-laden version wouldn't actually count as a low-capacity entry by this module's definition.

prompt: A person wants to build a library entry that turns out, on reflection, to be needed only once — a very specific, unusual negotiation they're unlikely to face again in that exact form. What's the soundest call?

options.text: Skip the library entry — a genuine one-off doesn't pay back the effort of saving and maintaining it, per lesson one's test
Save it anyway — every prompt is worth keeping just in case
Automate it fully instead of just saving the prompt

hints: Does this task pass lesson one's repetition-and-consistent-shape test, or not?
"Just in case" is exactly the instinct that leads to a rotting library full of entries nobody actually reuses.
explanation: A genuine one-off fails lesson one's test outright — it won't recur in a similar enough shape for a saved version to pay back the effort of writing, and later maintaining, it. "Save it just in case" is precisely the instinct that produces the kind of bloated, half-relevant library lesson four warned against — a library is healthier with fewer, genuinely reused entries than with everything that was ever written once.

prompt: For a capstone project, someone is choosing between: (A) a genuinely impressive multi-agent system for a problem they don't actually have, built mostly to look good, and (B) a plain script that would fix a mildly annoying but real weekly task they've had for a year. Which is the sounder capstone choice, and why?

options.text: A — a more sophisticated build demonstrates more skill regardless of whether the problem is real

B — a real, if modest, problem lets every later step (testing on real cases, measuring actual benefit) mean something, where a fabricated problem can't be genuinely tested or measured against real use
Neither — capstones should always be entirely new ideas, not existing annoyances

hints: Which one could you actually run against real, messy input and measure a real before/after on?
Module one's whole first lesson was about matching the pattern to the real task — the same discipline applies to picking the capstone's task itself.
explanation: B is the sounder choice, and for a specific reason beyond "simpler is safer": a real problem is the only kind that lets the rest of the phase's skills mean anything. You can only test against real messy cases (lesson three) and measure genuine before/after benefit (lesson four) if the problem was real to begin with — a fabricated problem for an impressive build has no real "before" to compare against, and no real user, including yourself, to tell you whether it actually helped.

prompt: Name a real, if modest, problem from your own work or life that you could plausibly solve with what this phase has covered (a chat pattern, a script, an automation, or a personal library entry). Say specifically who has this problem (even if it's just you), how often it comes up, and why it's been left unsolved so far.
hints: The strongest capstone candidates are usually the small annoyances that have quietly persisted for months, not the ambitious ideas that sound impressive on paper.
"Why has it been left unsolved" often reveals whether it's actually a good capstone fit — sometimes the honest answer is "it never occurred to me this was solvable," which is a great sign.
explanation: There's no single correct answer, but a strong response names a specific, real, recurring problem — not a hypothetical one — with a real person who has it (even if that's the author) and an honest reason it's persisted, which is often simply that nobody had connected it to something learnable, rather than that it was too hard.

prompt: Someone starts building their capstone immediately after choosing the problem, without writing down what "it worked" will actually mean. Two weeks in, they have something running but can't say whether it's actually better than before — just that it "feels okay." What step did they skip?

options.text: Defining, before building, what would actually count as success — a specific check, not a feeling
Choosing a more powerful AI model
Getting feedback from other people before starting

hints: "Feels okay" is exactly what happens when nobody defined a concrete check before starting.
This is the same principle as a lab's rubric, seen throughout this phase — a rubric written before starting, not invented after.
explanation: The missing step is defining success up front — a specific, checkable target (time saved, error rate, a before/after comparison) decided before building, not a vague sense arrived at afterward. Without that, "it worked" collapses into "it feels okay," which can't actually be verified or defended to anyone, including yourself in six months.

prompt: For the problem you named in lesson one (or a similar real one), name: which of the four patterns from this phase's first module fits it, one honest cost estimate using this phase's third module's method, and one specific, checkable definition of success you'd commit to before building anything.
hints: The pattern choice should be defended against its neighbours, not just asserted.
"Success" needs to be something you could actually check afterward, not a feeling — a number, a before/after comparison, a specific test passing.
explanation: A strong answer names a specific pattern (chat, script, automation, or a saved template) with a one-line justification against a neighbouring option, a rough cost estimate with any guessed numbers labelled honestly, and a success definition specific enough to check later — something like "saves at least 15 minutes a week, measured by timing myself doing it the old way once more for comparison" rather than "makes things easier."

prompt: Someone builds their capstone and tests it against three tidy examples they wrote themselves, all working perfectly. They declare it done. What's the risk, given this phase's earlier lessons?

options.text: None — three passing tests is enough to trust anything
Self-written tidy examples don't reveal how it handles messy, unexpected real input — the same gap module two's no-code lesson warned about
The risk only applies to no-code tools, not to a capstone project

hints: Who chose the three test examples, and did they resemble the messiest real case this will actually face?
This gap doesn't disappear just because the builder is more careful — it's about what kind of input was tested, not who did the testing.
explanation: Self-written, tidy test cases prove the basic mechanism works — they say nothing about how it handles the genuinely messy, unexpected input real use will eventually produce, which is exactly the gap this phase's earlier lesson on no-code tools named. The fix isn't more tidy tests; it's deliberately testing against the messiest, most awkward real case you can find or construct before calling it done.

prompt: Put these into the order that actually tests a capstone build properly before trusting it.

items: Test with a couple of clean, straightforward real examples to confirm the basic approach works
Deliberately test with the messiest, most unusual real case you can find or construct
Check what happens when a required input is missing or malformed
Only then consider it ready for real, ongoing use

hints: Clean examples confirm the wiring; messy and malformed cases test resilience — and resilience testing has to happen before the "ready for real use" declaration, not after.
explanation: This is the same order module two's failure-handling lesson established: confirm basic function with clean cases first, then deliberately stress it with messy and malformed input, and only declare it ready once both have been checked — not after the first clean pass alone.

prompt: A capstone builder says "it definitely saves me time" but has never actually timed the old manual way or the new AI-assisted way. What's missing from this claim?

options.text: A real before/after comparison — an actual measurement, not an impression, of how long each way takes
Nothing — a strong feeling that it's faster is sufficient evidence
The AI needs to be faster in general, which settles the question

hints: "Definitely" is doing a lot of work for a claim with no actual numbers behind it.
General AI speed doesn't answer whether this specific task, this specific way, is actually faster in practice.
explanation: The claim is missing an actual measurement — timing the old manual approach once, and the new approach once, gives a real before/after number instead of an impression, which can be wrong in either direction: people sometimes feel something is faster when reviewing and correcting AI output actually took as long as doing it by hand, and sometimes underestimate a genuine, large time saving because it doesn't feel dramatic day to day.

prompt: Sort each proposed measurement of a capstone's benefit by whether it's a genuine, checkable measurement or just a restated feeling.

items.text: Timing the manual process once and the AI-assisted process once, and comparing the two numbers
"It just feels a lot smoother now"
Counting how many of the last 20 outputs needed a manual correction before being usable
"I'm pretty sure it's better overall"

hints: A genuine measurement produces a number or a specific, checkable fact someone else could verify. A feeling doesn't, however confidently it's stated.
explanation: Timing both approaches and counting correction rates both produce a specific, checkable number — something a sceptical friend could ask to see and be shown. "Feels smoother" and "pretty sure it's better" are confidently stated but produce nothing checkable, which is exactly the gap between an impression and a measurement this lesson is about.

prompt: Six months after finishing a capstone, its builder can't remember why they chose the approach they did, what it actually cost, or whether they're still using it. What would have prevented this?

options.text: An honest write-up at the time — problem, approach and why, cost, what was measured, and whether it's still in use
Nothing — forgetting details after six months is unavoidable
Using a more memorable project name

hints: This mirrors module four's lesson on sharing a library entry with someone else — except here, the "someone else" reading it later is your own future self.
explanation: A written record — capturing the problem, the chosen approach and why, the actual or estimated cost, what was measured, and an honest note on whether it's still in use — is exactly what module four's sharing lesson argued for, except the audience here is your own future self just as much as anyone else. Without it, even a genuinely successful project becomes unreconstructable six months later.

prompt: Write the short version of your capstone's write-up: the problem in one sentence, the approach and why in one or two sentences, the rough cost, what you measured, and an honest one-line verdict on whether you're actually still using it (or would, if it's not finished yet).
hints: This should be short enough that someone with 30 seconds could read it and understand what you built and whether it worked.
An honest verdict is more valuable than a flattering one — "I stopped using it after two weeks because X" is a genuinely useful thing to have written down.
explanation: There's no fixed correct content, but a strong write-up is honest and specific rather than promotional: it states plainly what problem was real, why this approach fit better than the obvious alternative, roughly what it cost, what was actually measured (not just claimed), and a genuinely honest verdict on ongoing use — including admitting if the honest answer is that it stopped being used, which is exactly the kind of information module four's library-maintenance lesson said is worth capturing rather than hiding.

prompt: A capstone candidate: "Build a comprehensive AI system to modernise how our entire industry handles customer service." What's the clearest issue by lesson one's test?

options.text: Too broad and not scoped to something finishable within the phase, and likely not a problem the author personally has and can test against real use
It's a perfectly good capstone as written
It doesn't mention a specific AI provider

hints: Could this realistically be finished, tested against real cases, and measured within this phase?
explanation: Industry-wide scope fails both the scoped and real-ownership tests — it's unlikely to be finishable within the phase, and "the entire industry" isn't a specific, real user the author can test against or measure genuine before/after benefit for.

prompt: Statement: "Once you've picked a good, real, scoped problem, you can go straight to building — the design step is optional if the problem is simple enough."

config.statement: Once you've picked a good, real, scoped problem, you can go straight to building — the design step is optional if the problem is simple enough.
config.rubric: A strong answer notes that even a simple problem needs a defined success check before building, or "did it work" collapses into an unverifiable feeling regardless of how simple the problem was.

hints: Does problem simplicity change whether you need a way to check if it worked afterward?
explanation: False — problem simplicity doesn't remove the need to define success up front. Even a simple, obviously-real problem leaves you unable to answer "did it work" with anything but a feeling if nobody decided, before building, what a checkable success would look like.

prompt: Order these testing steps for a capstone build.

items: Test with a couple of clean, straightforward real examples
Deliberately test with the messiest real case available
Check behaviour on missing or malformed input
Declare it ready for real use

hints: Clean tests confirm the mechanism; messy and malformed tests confirm resilience — resilience testing has to come before declaring readiness.
explanation: Clean examples first confirm the basic approach functions; messy and malformed cases then test what a real deployment will actually face, and only after both should something be called ready — the order mirrors module two's failure-handling sequence directly.

prompt: A builder claims their capstone "clearly saves a lot of time" but has no timed comparison. What's the soundest next step?

options.text: Time the old manual approach once and the new approach once, and compare the actual numbers
Trust the claim — confident impressions are usually accurate
Assume it's fine since AI tools are generally faster

hints: What would actually let someone else verify this claim?
explanation: A single timed comparison of both approaches turns an unverifiable impression into a checkable number — exactly the gap lesson four is about, and confident impressions of time saved are exactly the kind of claim that sometimes turns out smaller (or larger) than expected once actually measured.

prompt: Sort each capstone write-up element by whether it belongs in an honest account or is the kind of thing that gets quietly left out of a flattering one.

items.text: The rough actual or estimated cost, even if higher than expected
An admission that part of it broke and was never fixed
A specific measured benefit, with the real number
A vague claim that it "went really well" with no specifics

hints: An honest write-up includes exactly the details a flattering one tends to smooth over.
explanation: Cost and real measured numbers belong in an honest account precisely because they're checkable and specific. Admissions that something broke, and vague unspecific claims of success, sit on opposite sides — one is honest but uncomfortable and often omitted, the other is comfortable but empty and often substituted in its place.

prompt: Critique a hypothetical capstone: someone built an agent to autonomously manage their entire personal email inbox, tested it only on emails they wrote themselves as examples, and reports "it's amazing" with no specific measurement. Name two specific weaknesses in this capstone, using this module's own criteria.
hints: Look at scope/pattern choice, testing method, and measurement — three separate places this example could be critiqued.
explanation: Two solid critiques: an autonomous agent managing an entire inbox is likely more machinery than most people's actual email judgement needs (module one's proportionality point), and testing only on self-written examples never checked how it handles real, messy incoming email (lesson three's gap) — combined with "it's amazing" being a feeling, not a measurement (lesson four). A genuinely strong critique names the specific gap, not just "this seems risky."

prompt: Which of these is the most honest, useful one-line capstone verdict?

options.text: "Saves about 20 minutes a week on average; the failure handling has caught two bad inputs so far and flagged them correctly; still in active use after three weeks"
"It's a total success and I'll never do this task manually again"
"AI is really powerful"

hints: Which one gives someone else something specific and checkable, rather than an impression?
explanation: The first gives specific, checkable claims — a time figure, a concrete example of failure handling working, and a real usage status — exactly what an honest write-up should contain. The other two are confident but contentless: neither could be verified or learned from by someone reading it later.
